title: Bbuga
author: Maama Nakato
desc: Red amaranth stewed down with carrot and green pepper in palm oil, thickened with a spoonful of groundnut paste and simmered until the liquid halves — the long treatment, where the green one gets the quick fry.
longDesc: Bbuga is the red amaranth, and it is a different proposition from dodo. These leaves have a raw earthy smell and a taste that can be off-putting straight out of the ground, and the answer is not to cook them fast but to stew them: palm oil, ginger, a thickening of groundnut paste, and half an hour of simmering that turns the earthiness into something round. It is the same plant family as dodo and they are not interchangeable in the pan.
equipment: Small bowl, for the groundnut paste
steps: Put the pan on high heat, add the palm oil and let it melt.
Add the garlic and onions and let them cook until translucent.
Add the tomatoes and cook until soft and tender.
Add the amaranth and stir well.
Toss in the carrots, green pepper, salt and pepper, and cover the pan.
In a bowl, loosen the groundnut paste with a little water until runny.
Add the paste to the stew, stirring as it goes in.
Add water or stock, cover, and let it boil for about 10 minutes.
Reduce the heat and simmer 20 to 30 minutes, until the liquid has reduced by half.
Take it off the heat and serve hot with your starch of choice.
chefTips: Do not treat bbuga like dodo. The red one wants stewing; the green one wants a two-minute fry. Swapping the methods gets you the worst of both.
The groundnut paste is the thickener and it must be loosened with water first. Spooned in dry it sits in lumps.
Palm oil rather than a neutral oil. It stands up to the earthiness in a way vegetable oil does not.
Simmering is what removes the raw earthy smell these leaves have. Half an hour is not too long.
The published source says 30 minutes on the blog and 20 in the author's own ebook, unreconciled. Anywhere in that range works — go by the liquid halving.
Ginger is doing real work here, not just seasoning. Do not leave it out.
Stock instead of water if you have it.
commonMistakes: Cooking it fast like dodo, leaving it earthy and raw-tasting.
Taking it off before the liquid has reduced.
sources: Adapted from Sophia Musoki, 'Red Amaranth (Bbuga) Stew', A Kitchen In Uganda (5 July 2017), also printed in her free ebook 16 Ugandan Dishes to Make (pp.21–22) — all quantities and the method are hers.
Her headnote that these vegetables have a raw earthy smell and a taste that is sometimes repulsive, and that the answer is groundnut thickening, ginger and palm oil, is from that post.
The 30-minute blog simmer against the 20-minute ebook simmer is her own unreconciled discrepancy, reproduced as printed.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Amaranth leaves are exceptionally high in vitamins A and C, iron, calcium and folate.
The red pigment comes with betalains, which are antioxidants.
Groundnut paste adds protein and the fat that helps the body absorb the carotenoids.
Contains peanuts — not suitable for anyone with a nut allergy.
culturalNote: Dodo and bbuga are the same plant in two colours and Ugandans treat them as different vegetables, which is the kind of distinction that gets flattened the moment a cuisine is written up by outsiders. The red one is the harder to like and the more interesting once it is cooked properly.
